screening_frequencies.name: Screening for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes in asymptomatic adults

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes in asymptomatic adults
screening_frequencies.applies_to: People with prediabetes (A1C ≥5.7% [≥39 mmol/mol], IGT, or IFG) should be tested yearly.

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes in asymptomatic adults
screening_frequencies.applies_to: People who were diagnosed with GDM should have testing at least every 1–3 years.

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes in asymptomatic adults
screening_frequencies.applies_to: If results are normal, testing should be repeated at a minimum of 3-year intervals, with consideration of more frequent testing depending on initial results and risk status.

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes in asymptomatic children and adolescents
screening_frequencies.applies_to: If tests are normal, repeat testing at a minimum of 3-year intervals (or more frequently if BMI is increasing or risk factor profile is deteriorating) is recommended.

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for type 1 diabetes risk
screening_frequencies.applies_to: Individuals with a single confirmed islet autoantibody should undergo repeat antibody testing every 6 months to 3 years (depending on age) to assess for persistence or seroconversion. E

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for hyperglycemia after organ transplantation
screening_frequencies.applies_to: people treated with ICIs, fasting or random plasma glucose should be tested before initiating treatment, during each visit, or if symptoms and signs of hyperglycemia develop during or after treatment cessation.

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for hyperglycemia with PI3Kα inhibitors
screening_frequencies.frequency: weekly for the first 2 weeks of treatment and then every 4 weeks
screening_frequencies.applies_to: In people treated with PI3Kα inhibitors, fasting or random plasma glucose should be tested before initiating treatment, and random plasma glucose should be tested weekly for the first 2 weeks of treatment and then every 4 weeks during treatment.

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for hyperglycemia with mTOR inhibitors
screening_frequencies.applies_to: In people treated with mTOR inhibitors, fasting or random plasma glucose should be tested before starting and at each visit throughout the duration of treatment.

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for GDM
screening_frequencies.applies_to: pregnant individuals not previously found to have diabetes or high-risk abnormal glucose metabolism detected earlier in the current pregnancy.

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for prediabetes or diabetes postpartum
screening_frequencies.applies_to: Individuals with GDM should be screened for prediabetes or diabetes at 4–12 weeks postpartum, using the 75-g OGTT and clinically appropriate non-pregnancy diagnostic criteria.

screening_frequencies.name: Lifelong screening for prediabetes or diabetes in individuals with a history of GDM
screening_frequencies.applies_to: Individuals with a history of GDM should have lifelong screening for the development of prediabetes or diabetes every 1–3 years.

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for undiagnosed diabetes in early pregnancy
screening_frequencies.applies_to: In individuals who are planning pregnancy, test those with risk factors (Table 2.5) B and consider testing all individuals of childbearing potential for undiagnosed prediabetes or diabetes at the first prenatal visit using standard diagnostic criteria if not screened preconception.

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for abnormal glucose metabolism in early pregnancy
screening_frequencies.applies_to: Before 15 weeks of gestation, test individuals with risk factors (Table 2.5) and consider testing all individuals for undiagnosed diabetes at the first prenatal visit using standard diagnostic criteria if not screened preconception.

Pancreatic diabetes (also termed pancreatogenic diabetes or type 3c diabetes) includes both structural (e.g., destruction or removal of normal pancreatic tissue) and functional loss of insulin secretion in the context of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and is commonly misdiagnosed as type 2 diabetes. The diverse set of etiologies includes pancreatitis (acute and chronic pancreatic inflammation and associated fibrosis leading to loss of functional exocrine and endocrine pancreatic function), cystic fibrosis, trauma or pancreatectomy, neoplasia, cystic fibrosis (addressed later in this section), hemochromatosis, fibrocalculous pancreatopathy, rare genetic disorders, and idiopathic forms (2); as such, pancreatic diabetes is the preferred umbrella term (136).

Several terms are used in the literature to describe the presence of diabetes following organ transplantation (157). New-onset diabetes after transplantation (NODAT) is one such designation that describes individuals who develop new-onset diabetes following transplant.
Specific types of diabetes due to other causes, e.g., monogenic diabetes syndromes, diseases of the exocrine pancreas, and drug- or chemical-induced diabetes
MODY is frequently characterized by onset of hyperglycemia at an early age (classically before age 25 years, although diagnosis may occur at older ages).

The introduction of immunotherapy, specifically immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), for cancer treatment has led to unexpected adverse events, including immune system activation precipitating autoimmune disease. Fulminant onset of autoimmune diabetes can occur with DKA and low or undetectable levels of C-peptide as a marker of endogenous β-cell function (64,65).
